title: WHERE YOU SPEND MOST OF YOUR TIME AND MONEY IS WHERE YOUR HEART IS
paragraphs: WHERE YOU SPEND MOST OF YOUR TIME AND MONEY IS WHERE YOUR HEART IS
The Quiet Audit Nobody Wants to Take
Most people think they know where their heart is.
They point to what they believe.
What they feel when worship music plays.
What they tell others matters most.
But Jesus offered a different measurement.
A measurement that cuts through self-deception, religious performance, and carefully crafted appearances.
It is not found in your words.
It is found in your calendar.
It is found in your bank statement.
It is found in your habits.
It is found in what receives your attention when nobody is watching.
And if we are honest, that truth can feel uncomfortable.
Because many of us say Jesus is first while our lives quietly testify otherwise.
Jesus addressed this issue directly during the Sermon on the Mount.
"Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."

ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου,
ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου.
(Hopou gar estin ho thēsauros sou, ekei estai kai hē kardia sou.)
"For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."
Jesus does not say your treasure follows your heart.
He says your heart follows your treasure.
Most people think they spend money on what they already love.
Jesus reveals that what we continually invest in begins to shape what we love.
Every expenditure becomes an act of devotion.
The question is not merely what do you love?
What are you training your heart to love?
The Hebrew Understanding of the Heart
Modern culture often treats the heart as a place of emotions.
Ancient Scripture viewed it very differently.
The Hebrew word for heart is:
In biblical thought, the heart was not merely the emotional center.
It was the control center of the entire person.
When Scripture speaks about your heart, it is speaking about the deepest source of who you are.
"Guard your heart above all else, for it is the source of life's consequences."
The heart is portrayed as the wellspring from which everything else flows.
Which means if your money and time continually move toward something, eventually your heart follows.
Not because God designed you poorly.
Because God designed you to become attached to whatever you continually treasure.
The Modern Idols Nobody Calls Idols
Most Christians would never bow before a golden statue.
Yet idolatry has always been less about statues and more about priorities.
An idol is whatever occupies the place only God deserves.
For others, the endless pursuit of more.
The tragedy is that idols rarely announce themselves.
And we discover we gave our best energy to things that could never save us.
The Scariest Receipt You Will Ever Read
Imagine for a moment that every dollar you spent this year and every hour you used was displayed publicly.
Would it reveal an increasing love for Christ?
Or would it expose a life consumed by temporary things?
That question is not intended to produce guilt.
It is intended to produce clarity.
Because clarity is often the first step toward repentance.
The Rich Young Ruler's Hidden God
One of the most heartbreaking encounters in the Gospels appears in Matthew 19.
A wealthy young ruler approached Jesus.
From the outside he appeared spiritually healthy.
Yet Jesus identified the one thing occupying God's place.
"Go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me."
Not because Jesus asked too much.
But because his possessions had already claimed ownership of his heart.
The issue was never money itself.
Scripture never teaches that wealth is inherently evil.
The money was not in his wallet.
The money was on his throne.
And Jesus refuses to share His throne.
Money is not the only indicator.
Time often tells an even more revealing story.
We all receive the same twenty-four hours.
And where we spend it often reveals what we truly value.
We find time for what matters.
The uncomfortable truth is not that we lack time.
And we wonder why our hearts feel distant from God.
Perhaps the answer is not mysterious.
Perhaps our hearts simply followed our investments.
The Early Church Understood Something We Have Forgotten
In Acts 2, believers displayed a radically different relationship with possessions.
They viewed everything through the lens of God's kingdom.
The Gospel had so transformed their hearts that they no longer viewed ownership the same way.
And when treasure changes, hearts follow.
Perhaps the most astonishing truth in Scripture is that God Himself demonstrates this principle.
What God treasures, God invests in.
And according to the Gospel, God invested His Son.
"For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son..."
Heaven's greatest investment was made for undeserving sinners.
The cross stands forever as proof of what God values.
And if God considered your salvation worth the blood of Christ, then your life was never meant to be spent chasing lesser treasures.
This is not an article about condemnation.
An invitation to perform an honest audit.
What am I teaching my heart to love?
He was exposing one of the deepest spiritual realities ever spoken.
Your heart is already following something.
The only question is whether it is following Christ.
Maybe it awakens something that has been asleep for years.
But if the Holy Spirit is revealing misplaced priorities, do not run from that conviction.
Conviction is not the voice of rejection.
It is the voice of mercy inviting you home.
The beautiful truth of the Gospel is that no matter how far your heart has wandered, Jesus still welcomes repentant sinners.
And the God who purchased you at Calvary is still worthy of first place.
So before you close this article, ask yourself honestly:
If someone examined where I spend most of my time and money, would they conclude that Jesus is my greatest treasure?
This question hits harder than most people expect.
One day your bank statement and your calendar will testify about what your mouth only claimed.
